record.paper_title: A Survey on LoRa Networking: Research Problems, Current Solutions and Open Issues
record.context_brief: Scenario-specific LoRa security and key management
record.original_question: What security architecture, key-management mechanisms, and per-application security requirements are needed to secure LoRa networks against remaining attacks such as node impersonation, eavesdropping, black-hole attacks, wormhole attacks, jamming, replay attacks, beacon-synchronization attacks, traffic analysis, man-in-the-middle attacks, and compromised keys? In deployment scenarios where the application service provider and the network service provider are different organizations, how should the Application Session Key and Network Session Key be generated, updated, separated, and kept confidential from the inappropriate party?

evidence.quote: Existing LoRa technology generates the key and never updates it. Hence, Key generation and Key update mechanism is a major concern. Third-party authorization is required when the application and network service providers are different. So, these applications require third-party authorization to ensure privacy and security [47], [75], [76].
LoRa devices are susceptible to jamming attack, replay attack, beacon synchronization attack, trafﬁc analysis and man-in-the-middle attack.

The network server and application server can derive both Application and Network session keys which is not secure if two different organizations are involved. So, a trusted third-party key management architecture is proposed.

Security spans over a range of attacks like node impersonation, eavesdropping, Black hole attack, Wormhole attack, etc., as discussed by Zhou et al. [86]. Only few key management techniques have been discussed and proposed for LoRa. Several attacks still need to be addressed to secure LoRa networks.

Even though some techniques enhance the security of existing LoRa standard, security requirements of LoRa are not discussed based on the applications of LoRa. In the future, each application of LoRa will demand their own security needs.

For example, some applications may require Network and Application Session keys to be independent and Network Session Key should be conﬁdential from application server and vice-versa. Hence, the security needs of each deploying scenario have to be deeply investigated to mitigate vulnerabilities arising due to different application scenarios.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a LoRaWAN-style low-power wide-area network consisting of: (i) a set of end devices D, (ii) one or more gateways, (iii) a Network Server (NS) operated by a network service provider, and (iv) an Application Server (AS) operated by an application service provider, where NS and AS may belong to distinct administrative organizations. Each end device d ∈ D shares two symmetric session keys: a Network Session Key NwkSKey_d (used for MAC-layer integrity/authentication between d and NS) and an Application Session Key AppSKey_d (used for end-to-end payload confidentiality between d and AS). In current deployments these keys are derived once (e.g., from a root key during a Join procedure) and are never refreshed, and both NS and AS are structurally able to compute, or have access to, both keys.

Design a security architecture and key-management protocol for such a network that simultaneously satisfies all of the following requirements:

1. Key separation and confidentiality across organizations: AppSKey_d must remain unknown to the NS, and NwkSKey_d must remain unknown to the AS, even though both servers participate in delivering each uplink/downlink frame.
2. Key generation and periodic key update: provide explicit mechanisms by which NwkSKey_d and AppSKey_d (and any underlying root keys) are generated at session establishment and rotated during the lifetime of a device, including rekeying triggers and synchronization between d, NS, and AS.
3. Optional trusted third-party authorization: specify how a trusted Key Management Server, distinct from NS and AS, can mediate join, key derivation, and key update so that neither NS nor AS learns the other's session key.
4. Resistance to the following attack classes, each of which must be formally characterized by an adversary model and against which the protocol must be proven (or argued) secure:
   (a) node impersonation, (b) passive eavesdropping, (c) black-hole attacks, (d) wormhole attacks, (e) jamming, (f) replay attacks, (g) beacon-synchronization attacks, (h) traffic analysis, (i) man-in-the-middle attacks, and (j) compromise of one or more session keys (forward and backward secrecy under key compromise).
5. Per-application differentiation: provide a methodology for tailoring the above mechanisms to the heterogeneous security requirements of distinct LoRa application classes (e.g., metering, healthcare, industrial control, smart agriculture), including how requirements such as confidentiality, integrity, availability, and privacy are quantified and mapped to concrete protocol parameters.

Produce such an architecture together with a security proof (or rigorous justification) of the claimed properties under standard cryptographic assumptions, and analyze its overhead in terms of the constrained energy, bandwidth, and duty-cycle budget characteristic of LoRa end devices.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent literature (2020–2025) on LoRaWAN security continues to propose partial solutions—e.g., third-party key management schemes, blockchain-based join procedures, and rekeying protocols—but no single architecture has been established that simultaneously addresses key separation between distinct network and application providers, periodic key update, and the full catalogue of attacks listed (jamming, wormhole, beacon-sync, traffic analysis, key compromise, etc.). Surveys consistently flag these as remaining open issues.

status_evidence.title: LoRaWAN Security: A Survey
status_evidence.snippet: Surveys LoRaWAN security weaknesses and notes that key management, key updating, and protection against jamming/replay/MITM remain open challenges.
status_evidence.claim: Multiple known attack vectors and key-update issues in LoRaWAN remain unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Survey on LoRaWAN security issues and solutions
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews proposed key-management and authentication schemes for LoRaWAN and identifies open problems including session-key separation when NS and AS belong to different organizations.
status_evidence.claim: No comprehensive scheme yet addresses all listed requirements simultaneously.
